concepts.title: Microbe Diversity and Culturing on Nutritive Media

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Microbe Diversity and Culturing on Nutritive Media' refers to.
questions.a: Microorganisms span protozoa, bacteria, fungi, microscopic plant and animal viruses, viroids and prions, thriving everywhere from hundred-degree thermal vents to acidic pools and deep soil; bacteria and many fungi can be raised on nutritive media into visible colonies, which is what makes laboratory study of them possible.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Microbe Diversity and Culturing on Nutritive Media'.
questions.a: Only a handful of microbes cause disease -- the vast majority are neutral or useful, and their tiny size hides an enormous metabolic range.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Microbe Diversity and Culturing on Nutritive Media' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 8.1 (introduction) (source: lebo108.txt lines 1-21 (microbe groups, extreme habitats, colony growth on media))

concepts.title: Microbes in Household Products: Curd, Dough and Cheese

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Microbes in Household Products: Curd, Dough and Cheese' refers to.
questions.a: Every kitchen runs on microbes: lactic acid bacteria such as lactobacillus turn milk into curd, their acids coagulating and partly digesting milk proteins while boosting vitamin b12 and checking pathogens in the stomach; bacterial fermentation puffs dosa and idli dough with carbon dioxide, baker's yeast raises bread, palm sap ferments into toddy, and propionibacterium sharmanii blows the holes into swiss cheese while a ripening fungus flavours roquefort.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Microbes in Household Products: Curd, Dough and Cheese'.
questions.a: A spoonful of curd works as starter (inoculum) because millions of lab cells carry the fermentation forward -- the same logic behind every traditional fermented food.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Microbes in Household Products: Curd, Dough and Cheese' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 8.1 (source: lebo108.txt lines 77-105 (curd/LAB, dosa-idli dough, bread, toddy, Swiss and Roquefort cheese))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Fermented Beverages and Brewer's Yeast' refers to.
questions.a: Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the same brewer's yeast used in bread, ferments malted cereals and fruit juices into ethanol on an industrial scale inside large vessels called fermentors; wine and beer stop at fermentation, while whisky, brandy and rum take the extra step of distilling the fermented broth.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Fermented Beverages and Brewer's Yeast'.
questions.a: One yeast, one reaction, two product families -- distillation is the only divide between wine-and-beer and whisky-brand-rum.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Fermented Beverages and Brewer's Yeast' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 8.2.1 (source: lebo108.txt lines 106-134 (fermentors, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, distilled versus undistilled drinks))

concepts.title: Antibiotics: Penicillin and the War on Bacteria

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Antibiotics: Penicillin and the War on Bacteria' refers to.
questions.a: Antibiotics are chemicals some microbes make to kill or stall other microbes -- against microbial life but pro human life; penicillin surfaced by chance when fleming noticed a penicillium notatum mould wiping out staphylococci on an unwashed plate, chain and florey later proved its full power, and the trio shared the 1945 nobel prize as the drug went on to tame plague, diphtheria, whooping cough and leprosy.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Antibiotics: Penicillin and the War on Bacteria'.
questions.a: A forgotten dirty plate opened the antibiotic era -- and after penicillin, purified antibiotics from many other microbes followed.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Antibiotics: Penicillin and the War on Bacteria' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 8.2.2 (source: lebo108.txt lines 135-168 (antibiotic definition, Fleming's discovery, Chain and Florey, WWII use, diseases controlled))

concepts.title: Industrial Chemicals, Enzymes and Bioactive Molecules

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Industrial Chemicals, Enzymes and Bioactive Molecules' refers to.
questions.a: Fermentor-grown microbes also supply organic acids (aspergillus niger for citric, acetobacter aceti for acetic, clostridium butylicum for butyric, lactobacillus for lactic), ethanol from yeast, working enzymes -- lipases for oily laundry stains, pectinases and proteases that clarify bottled juices, streptokinase as a clot buster after heart attacks -- and medicines such as cyclosporin a from trichoderma polysporum for transplant patients plus statins from monascus purpureus that competitively block cholesterol synthesis.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Industrial Chemicals, Enzymes and Bioactive Molecules'.
questions.a: Match the product to its maker -- each acid, enzyme and drug has one named microbe, and examiners love that pairing.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Industrial Chemicals, Enzymes and Bioactive Molecules' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 8.2.3 (source: lebo108.txt lines 169-190 (acid producers, lipases, pectinases, streptokinase, cyclosporin A, statins))

concepts.title: Sewage Treatment: Primary, Secondary Stages and BOD

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Sewage Treatment: Primary, Secondary Stages and BOD' refers to.
questions.a: Municipal waste water, or sewage, is scrubbed in two stages at treatment plants: primary treatment removes particles physically by sequential filtration and sedimentation, giving primary sludge and an effluent; secondary treatment aerates that effluent so heterotrophic microbes in flocs eat the organic matter, cutting the biochemical oxygen demand until flocs settle as activated sludge, part of which recycles to the aeration tank while the rest feeds anaerobic digesters that release methane-rich biogas.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Sewage Treatment: Primary, Secondary Stages and BOD'.
questions.a: Bod is the yardstick of pollution -- the oxygen microbes would need to oxidise a litre's organic load -- and treatment runs until that number drops enough for rivers to cope.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Sewage Treatment: Primary, Secondary Stages and BOD' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 8.3 (source: lebo108.txt lines 191-271 (primary/secondary treatment, flocs, BOD, activated sludge, digesters, Ganga and Yamuna action plans))

concepts.title: Biogas: Methanogens and the Gobar Gas Plant

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Biogas: Methanogens and the Gobar Gas Plant' refers to.
questions.a: Methanogens -- anaerobic bacteria such as methanobacterium that grow on cellulosic material -- emit plentiful methane alongside carbon dioxide and hydrogen, making biogas; they flourish in sewage sludge and in the rumen of cattle where they help digest cellulose, so cattle dung (gobar) seeds the typical biogas plant: a 10-15 feet concrete tank of slurry under a floating cover whose pipe delivers cooking and lighting gas, with spent slurry out as fertiliser.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Biogas: Methanogens and the Gobar Gas Plant'.
questions.a: The rumen connection explains everything -- the same cellulose-digesting methanogens that help cattle digest make gobar gas possible.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Biogas: Methanogens and the Gobar Gas Plant' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 8.4 (source: lebo108.txt lines 272-324 (methanogens, rumen, gobar gas, plant design, IARI and KVIC))

concepts.title: Biocontrol: Ladybirds, Bt, Trichoderma and Baculoviruses

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Biocontrol: Ladybirds, Bt, Trichoderma and Baculoviruses' refers to.
questions.a: Biocontrol manages pests with living agents instead of toxic chemicals: ladybird beetles eat aphids and dragonflies hunt mosquitoes; bacillus thuringiensis spores sprayed on brassicas die inside caterpillar guts releasing their toxin; the free-living root fungus trichoderma fights several plant pathogens; and nucleopolyhedrovirus baculoviruses give species-specific, narrow-spectrum control that leaves beneficial insects unharmed -- ideal for organic farming and integrated pest management.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Biocontrol: Ladybirds, Bt, Trichoderma and Baculoviruses'.
questions.a: Organic farming keeps pests at manageable levels through ecological checks and balances rather than eradicating them -- predators need prey to survive too.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Biocontrol: Ladybirds, Bt, Trichoderma and Baculoviruses' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 8.5 (source: lebo108.txt lines 325-386 (organic farming logic, Ladybird, Dragonflies, Bt, Trichoderma, Nucleopolyhedrovirus, IPM))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Biofertilisers: Rhizobium, Mycorrhiza and Cyanobacteria' refers to.
questions.a: Biofertilisers are organisms that enrich soil nutrients, easing the pollution burden of chemical fertilisers: rhizobium in legume root nodules and free-living azospirillum or azotobacter fix atmospheric nitrogen into usable organic forms; glomus mycorrhizal fungi absorb phosphorus for the plant and earn resistance to root pathogens plus salinity and drought tolerance in return; and cyanobacteria such as anabaena, nostoc and oscillatoria fix nitrogen in paddy fields while adding organic matter.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Biofertilisers: Rhizobium, Mycorrhiza and Cyanobacteria'.
questions.a: Symbiosis does the fertilising -- bacteria trade nitrogen, fungi trade phosphorus, and both draw sugars from the plant partner.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Biofertilisers: Rhizobium, Mycorrhiza and Cyanobacteria' taught, and from which source text?
